texts.orig: This is a common challenge Product Managers face. They want to create cross-functional teams to leverage a diverse set of skills and perspectives and yet when they bring folks together from various disciplines, those differences often create tension.
texts.text: This is a common challenge Product Managers face. They want to create cross-functional teams to leverage a diverse set of skills and perspectives and yet when they bring folks together from various disciplines, those differences often create tension.

texts.label: text

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 1. Define metrics together
texts.text: 1. Define metrics together

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Designers and engineers are most engaged when they are involved in goal setting and goal breakdown. Sometimes product managers hesitate to “waste people’s time” in sessions about goals, but I would argue it is the most valuable time to spend together.
texts.text: Designers and engineers are most engaged when they are involved in goal setting and goal breakdown. Sometimes product managers hesitate to “waste people’s time” in sessions about goals, but I would argue it is the most valuable time to spend together.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When you define quarterly goals, invite your whole team to participate.
texts.text: When you define quarterly goals, invite your whole team to participate.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Use the time to reflect on how you did last quarter and consider where to focus this quarter. Here’s a sample working session agenda:
texts.text: Use the time to reflect on how you did last quarter and consider where to focus this quarter. Here’s a sample working session agenda:

texts.orig: During these conversations, check in with your teammates. Do they seem excited and engaged? If not, try to figure out what gets them excited about working on this team.
texts.text: During these conversations, check in with your teammates. Do they seem excited and engaged? If not, try to figure out what gets them excited about working on this team.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I once worked with an extraordinary engineer who was really passionate about performance. We worked to connect the dots from performance to conversion to see if we could prove meaningful impact. Through this work, we could both stay focused on the business goals and tie into elements that mattered to engineering and design.
texts.text: I once worked with an extraordinary engineer who was really passionate about performance. We worked to connect the dots from performance to conversion to see if we could prove meaningful impact. Through this work, we could both stay focused on the business goals and tie into elements that mattered to engineering and design.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 2. Review metrics together
texts.text: 2. Review metrics together

texts.label: text
texts.orig: One thing I see quite often is that designers and engineers do not have easy access to the metrics they are being held accountable for. Either, they don’t have access at all, or they have access but don’t really know what to look for.
texts.text: One thing I see quite often is that designers and engineers do not have easy access to the metrics they are being held accountable for. Either, they don’t have access at all, or they have access but don’t really know what to look for.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You can address this by reviewing your team metrics together. And often.
texts.text: You can address this by reviewing your team metrics together. And often.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Show what dashboards or charts you look at and explain how they tie into your quarterly goals or company health overall. Be patient and encourage questions.
texts.text: Show what dashboards or charts you look at and explain how they tie into your quarterly goals or company health overall. Be patient and encourage questions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It’s also really powerful when you can connect the dots from their work to their impact. Show a recent experiment or release and explain how the work created change (or didn’t). Ask the team to reflect on why. Involve them as you plan the next steps. Celebrate big wins with the team and when things don’t go so well, take the time to have thoughtful conversations about your decisions.
texts.text: It’s also really powerful when you can connect the dots from their work to their impact. Show a recent experiment or release and explain how the work created change (or didn’t). Ask the team to reflect on why. Involve them as you plan the next steps. Celebrate big wins with the team and when things don’t go so well, take the time to have thoughtful conversations about your decisions.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When you review data with the team, you may also surface their interest in getting more into analytics. Help connect your teammates with resources or access so they too can explore their impact confidently.
texts.text: When you review data with the team, you may also surface their interest in getting more into analytics. Help connect your teammates with resources or access so they too can explore their impact confidently.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 3. Prioritize together
texts.text: 3. Prioritize together

texts.label: text
texts.orig: I like to start prioritization sessions by reviewing the team goals and how we are tracking against them. When you bring the goals and metrics forward each week, it helps everyone remember what we should be working on. And it makes it harder to go to bat for a low impact task.
texts.text: I like to start prioritization sessions by reviewing the team goals and how we are tracking against them. When you bring the goals and metrics forward each week, it helps everyone remember what we should be working on. And it makes it harder to go to bat for a low impact task.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: As you prioritize projects, experiments or stories, make room for your team to voice what they think is high impact. But also, challenge them on it. Say a designer wants to work on a navigation redesign - ask them how the navigation is doing today. Ask them how they would measure success for the business, or for the user. Ask them to make a case.
texts.text: As you prioritize projects, experiments or stories, make room for your team to voice what they think is high impact. But also, challenge them on it. Say a designer wants to work on a navigation redesign - ask them how the navigation is doing today. Ask them how they would measure success for the business, or for the user. Ask them to make a case.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: Not everything will have a measurable impact, so you have to make a judgment call about what to push back on. Do so thoughtfully and carefully and without targeting any one individual. It’s important that everyone be upheld to the same standard on this--even PMs. Everyone should be able to explain why they want to prioritize something, what evidence they have for impact and how success should be evaluated. And occasionally, if someone really cares about something and it takes a couple of hours, let them do it. Respect what your teammates value and they will respect what you value.
texts.text: Not everything will have a measurable impact, so you have to make a judgment call about what to push back on. Do so thoughtfully and carefully and without targeting any one individual. It’s important that everyone be upheld to the same standard on this--even PMs. Everyone should be able to explain why they want to prioritize something, what evidence they have for impact and how success should be evaluated. And occasionally, if someone really cares about something and it takes a couple of hours, let them do it. Respect what your teammates value and they will respect what you value.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: 4. Reflect on releases together
texts.text: 4. Reflect on releases together

texts.label: text
texts.orig: When you ship something, review how it has performed together. Talk about what was prioritized in this release and what wasn’t and whether or not that made a difference. Discuss what worked well and what didn’t.
texts.text: When you ship something, review how it has performed together. Talk about what was prioritized in this release and what wasn’t and whether or not that made a difference. Discuss what worked well and what didn’t.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: It helps if you document how you’re measuring success in a product or experiment plan before the release. Make sure your team is clear on what success means and evaluate together whether or not something was successful. Consider what you all might do differently next time.
texts.text: It helps if you document how you’re measuring success in a product or experiment plan before the release. Make sure your team is clear on what success means and evaluate together whether or not something was successful. Consider what you all might do differently next time.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: You can also try shipping some of the projects or improvements your engineers and designers are really fighting for. Give them a win. Define success together and review the impact together. Either they will see that they are pushing for the wrong thing or you will find out that they were right all along.

Define success together and review the impact together. Either they will see that they are pushing for the wrong thing or you will find out that they were right all along.

texts.label: section_header
texts.orig: Q: I am a data scientist looking to make the switch to product. What are your thoughts on internal tracks from DS/design/eng to product, and how to best leverage my data science background in modeling and experimentation when I do so? Also, I’ve heard that the transition to PM internally will potentially result in a “demotion” to the base level for PMs so it’s better off transitioning to PM in a new company. Is this true and how would you advise I approach this.
texts.text: Q: I am a data scientist looking to make the switch to product. What are your thoughts on internal tracks from DS/design/eng to product, and how to best leverage my data science background in modeling and experimentation when I do so? Also, I’ve heard that the transition to PM internally will potentially result in a “demotion” to the base level for PMs so it’s better off transitioning to PM in a new company. Is this true and how would you advise I approach this.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: If your goal is to break into Product Management,
texts.text: If your goal is to break into Product Management,

texts.label: text

texts.text: If you know you want to get in PM and your company offers a route there, don’t squander it.

If you’re having to move down multiple levels, I’d push back to understand the rationale. If nothing else, get a clear sense of what your new manager will need to see in order to quickly move up a level.

texts.label: text
texts.orig: In terms of how to actually land the gig, having a DS background is both a superpower and a liability. As a DS, you’re probably strong at many of the hard skills (e.g. driving impact, prioritization, execution, strategy), but less experienced with the weird soft-skills of the PM role (e.g. influence, product taste, keeping a team you aren’t managing happy and productive). My advice is to leverage your strengths, and fill in your gaps:
texts.text: In terms of how to actually land the gig, having a DS background is both a superpower and a liability. My advice is to leverage your strengths, and fill in your gaps:

texts.orig: Finally, closely observe the PMs that you work with day-to-day and identify what they do that is effective and ineffective. Then, try to model and avoid these things, respectively.
